Lecture 25

Convolution, correlation and integral equations

We prove the convolution theorem, Plancherel’s identity for bounded integrable functions and the correlation theorem, and we solve a convolution integral equation whose multiplier has no real zero.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Convert a convolution into a product of transforms, keep the factor 2π\sqrt{2\pi}2π​ of the convention, and state the hypotheses under which the conversion and the uniqueness of the transform hold.
  • Compute the output of a filter from its impulse response, and read its effect from the transfer factor.
  • Compute energies by Plancherel’s identity and correlations with the conjugation on the first function, and relate an autocorrelation to the squared modulus of the spectrum.
  • Prove uniqueness for a convolution integral equation whose multiplier does not vanish on the real axis, and solve it with a resolvent kernel.

Lecture 24 noted that the transform of a product is not the product of the transforms. A linear device that responds to a short input with a fixed response produces, for a general input, a superposition of shifted responses, a convolution. In this lecture we prove that the Fourier transform turns a convolution into a product, and we use this for a filter and for an integral equation. We also compare a signal with its spectrum, and two signals with each other.

25.1 Convolution

Throughout this lecture the functions are signals f(t)f(t)f(t) of the time ttt, and their transforms use the convention of Lecture 23 with the angular frequency ω\omegaω, f^(ω)=F ⁣[f](ω)=(2π)−1/2∫Re−iωtf(t) ⁣dt\widehat f(\omega)=\FT{f}(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\R}\ee^{-\iu\omega t}f(t)\dd tf​(ω)=F[f](ω)=(2π)−1/2∫R​e−iωtf(t)dt. Everything holds in space with xxx, ξ\xiξ and kkk for ttt, τ\tauτ and ω\omegaω. As in Lecture 23, a function is integrable on R\RR if it is piecewise continuous on every bounded interval and ∫R∣f∣ ⁣dt<∞\int_{\R}\abs f\dd t<\infty∫R​∣f∣dt<∞.

A linear device that is the same at all times, such as the RC circuit of Section 25.3, answers an impulse of unit strength at the time τ\tauτ with a response h(t−τ)h(t-\tau)h(t−τ). An input fff is approximately a sum of short impulses f(τ)Δτf(\tau)\Delta\tauf(τ)Δτ, so by superposition the response is approximately the sum of h(t−τ)f(τ)Δτh(t-\tau)f(\tau)\Delta\tauh(t−τ)f(τ)Δτ, and in the limit the integral ∫h(t−τ)f(τ) ⁣dτ\int h(t-\tau)f(\tau)\dd\tau∫h(t−τ)f(τ)dτ. This heuristic motivates the following definition.

Definition 25.1 (Convolution). Let fff be integrable on R\RR, and let ggg be bounded and integrable on R\RR. The convolution of fff and ggg is the function f∗gf\conv gf∗g given by (f∗g)(t)=∫Rf(τ) g(t−τ) ⁣dτ(t∈R).(f\conv g)(t)=\int_{\R}f(\tau)\,g(t-\tau)\dd\tau\qquad(t\in\R).(f∗g)(t)=∫R​f(τ)g(t−τ)dτ(t∈R).(25.1)

The variable τ\tauτ is the source time, as in the kernels of Part I.

As in Lectures 23 and 24, each use of the standing rules I1–I3 of Lecture 22 (dominated limits, with I1(b) for a continuous parameter; differentiation under the integral sign; Fubini–Tonelli) names the rule. Rule I3 allows discontinuities along lines τ=const\tau=\mathrm{const}τ=const and t−τ=constt-\tau=\mathrm{const}t−τ=const, as convolutions need.

A signal that vanishes for negative times is called causal. If fff and ggg are causal, then f(τ)=0f(\tau)=0f(τ)=0 for τ<0\tau<0τ<0 and g(t−τ)=0g(t-\tau)=0g(t−τ)=0 for τ>t\tau>tτ>t, so for t>0t>0t>0 (f∗g)(t)=∫0tf(τ) g(t−τ) ⁣dτ,(f\conv g)(t)=\int_0^tf(\tau)\,g(t-\tau)\dd\tau ,(f∗g)(t)=∫0t​f(τ)g(t−τ)dτ, and (f∗g)(t)=0(f\conv g)(t)=0(f∗g)(t)=0 for t<0t<0t<0. This causal form returns in Lecture 26.

Proposition 25.2 (Properties of the convolution). Let fff be integrable on R\RR, and let ggg be bounded and integrable on R\RR. Then the integral (25.1) converges absolutely for every t∈Rt\in\Rt∈R, and f∗gf\conv gf∗g is continuous on R\RR, with ∣(f∗g)(t)∣≤sup⁡R∣g∣∫R∣f∣ ⁣dτ,∫R∣f∗g∣ ⁣dt≤∫R∣f∣ ⁣dτ∫R∣g∣ ⁣dv.\abs{(f\conv g)(t)}\le\sup_{\R}\abs g\int_{\R}\abs f\dd\tau,\qquad \int_{\R}\abs{f\conv g}\dd t\le\int_{\R}\abs f\dd\tau\int_{\R}\abs g\dd v .∣(f∗g)(t)∣≤Rsup​∣g∣∫R​∣f∣dτ,∫R​∣f∗g∣dt≤∫R​∣f∣dτ∫R​∣g∣dv.(25.2) So f∗gf\conv gf∗g is bounded and integrable. If fff is also bounded, then f∗g=g∗ff\conv g=g\conv ff∗g=g∗f.

Proof. First, τ↦f(τ)g(t−τ)\tau\mapsto f(\tau)g(t-\tau)τ↦f(τ)g(t−τ) is piecewise continuous, with exceptional points at those of fff and at ttt minus those of ggg. Those excluded values of τ\tauτ form an exceptional set. The integrand is bounded by sup⁡∣g∣ ∣f(τ)∣\sup\abs g\,\abs{f(\tau)}sup∣g∣∣f(τ)∣ for every ttt. The convolution is continuous even when fff and ggg have jumps, as Example 25.6 shows for a pulse.

25.2 The convolution theorem

The transform turns a convolution into a product.

Theorem 25.3 (Convolution theorem). Let fff be integrable on R\RR, and let ggg be bounded and integrable on R\RR. Then for every ω∈R\omega\in\Rω∈R F ⁣[f∗g](ω)=2π f^(ω) g^(ω).\FT{f\conv g}(\omega)=\sqrt{2\pi}\,\widehat f(\omega)\,\widehat g(\omega) .F[f∗g](ω)=2π​f​(ω)g​(ω).(25.4)

Proof. By Proposition 25.2, f∗gf\conv gf∗g is integrable, so its transform exists. Fix ω\omegaω and consider the function (t,τ)↦e−iωtf(τ)g(t−τ)(t,\tau)\mapsto\ee^{-\iu\omega t}f(\tau)g(t-\tau)(t,τ)↦e−iωtf(τ)g(t−τ) on R2\R^2R2. Its modulus is the function of the proof of Proposition 25.2, whose iterated integral is finite, and it is continuous off the same lines. The inner integrals of the modulus were found there to be piecewise continuous. For fixed τ\tauτ, the substitution t=τ+vt=\tau+vt=τ+v gives the inner integral ∫Re−iωtf(τ)g(t−τ) ⁣dt=e−iωτf(τ)∫Re−iωvg(v) ⁣dv=2π g^(ω) e−iωτf(τ),\int_{\R}\ee^{-\iu\omega t}f(\tau)g(t-\tau)\dd t =\ee^{-\iu\omega\tau}f(\tau)\int_{\R}\ee^{-\iu\omega v}g(v)\dd v =\sqrt{2\pi}\,\widehat g(\omega)\,\ee^{-\iu\omega\tau}f(\tau),∫R​e−iωtf(τ)g(t−τ)dt=e−iωτf(τ)∫R​e−iωvg(v)dv=2π​g​(ω)e−iωτf(τ), which is piecewise continuous in τ\tauτ. For fixed ttt the inner integral is e−iωt(f∗g)(t)\ee^{-\iu\omega t}(f\conv g)(t)e−iωt(f∗g)(t), continuous in ttt. By rule I3 the two iterated integrals agree: ∫Re−iωt(f∗g)(t) ⁣dt=2π g^(ω)∫Re−iωτf(τ) ⁣dτ=2π g^(ω) 2π f^(ω).\int_{\R}\ee^{-\iu\omega t}(f\conv g)(t)\dd t =\sqrt{2\pi}\,\widehat g(\omega)\int_{\R}\ee^{-\iu\omega\tau}f(\tau)\dd\tau =\sqrt{2\pi}\,\widehat g(\omega)\,\sqrt{2\pi}\,\widehat f(\omega) .∫R​e−iωt(f∗g)(t)dt=2π​g​(ω)∫R​e−iωτf(τ)dτ=2π​g​(ω)2π​f​(ω). Dividing by 2π\sqrt{2\pi}2π​ gives (25.4). ■

The factor 2π\sqrt{2\pi}2π​ appears because the transform of f∗gf\conv gf∗g is a double integral with one factor (2π)−1/2(2\pi)^{-1/2}(2π)−1/2, while f^ g^\widehat f\,\widehat gf​g​ has two. In the non-unitary convention F=2π f^F=\sqrt{2\pi}\,\widehat fF=2π​f​ of Lecture 23’s card the theorem reads Ff∗g=FfFgF_{f\conv g}=F_fF_gFf∗g​=Ff​Fg​, without a factor. Some texts keep the unitary transform and put a factor (2π)−1/2(2\pi)^{-1/2}(2π)−1/2 into the convolution instead; their formulas are converted before they are combined with ours.

The convolution theorem becomes a method once a transform determines its function. The next proposition proves this from the results of Lectures 22 and 24.

Proposition 25.4 (Uniqueness of the transform). Let fff and ggg be integrable on R\RR with f^(ω)=g^(ω)\widehat f(\omega)=\widehat g(\omega)f​(ω)=g​(ω) for every ω∈R\omega\in\Rω∈R. Then f(t)=g(t)f(t)=g(t)f(t)=g(t) at every ttt at which f−gf-gf−g is continuous. In particular, if fff and ggg are continuous, then f=gf=gf=g.

Proof. Put d=f−gd=f-gd=f−g. It is integrable and d^=0\widehat d=0d=0. Let φ\varphiφ be a test function in D(R)\testspace(\R)D(R). It is rapidly decreasing, and Lecture 24 proved that the transform maps S(R)\Schwartz(\R)S(R) onto itself. So φ=ψ^\varphi=\widehat\psiφ=ψ​ for some ψ∈S(R)\psi\in\Schwartz(\R)ψ∈S(R), and ψ\psiψ is integrable. Lecture 24’s multiplication formula gives ∫Rd(t)φ(t) ⁣dt=∫Rd(t)ψ^(t) ⁣dt=∫Rd^(ω)ψ(ω) ⁣dω=0.\int_{\R}d(t)\varphi(t)\dd t=\int_{\R}d(t)\widehat\psi(t)\dd t=\int_{\R}\widehat d(\omega)\psi(\omega)\dd\omega=0 .∫R​d(t)φ(t)dt=∫R​d(t)ψ​(t)dt=∫R​d(ω)ψ(ω)dω=0. So the regular distribution of ddd is zero, and Lecture 22’s proposition on equal distributions gives d(t)=0d(t)=0d(t)=0 at every ttt at which ddd is continuous. ■

Values at the exceptional points cannot be recovered from the transform (Lecture 23).

To differentiate a convolution, we differentiate the factor that has a continuous derivative.

Proposition 25.7 (Derivative of a convolution). Let fff be integrable on R\RR, and let ggg be continuously differentiable on R\RR with ggg and g′g'g′ bounded and integrable. Then f∗gf\conv gf∗g is continuously differentiable, and (f∗g)′=f∗g′(f\conv g)'=f\conv g'(f∗g)′=f∗g′.

Proof. For each ttt the integrand f(τ)g(t−τ)f(\tau)g(t-\tau)f(τ)g(t−τ) is piecewise continuous in τ\tauτ, with the exceptional points of fff, which do not depend on ttt. Its derivative with respect to ttt is f(τ)g′(t−τ)f(\tau)g'(t-\tau)f(τ)g′(t−τ). This derivative is continuous in ttt, piecewise continuous in τ\tauτ, and bounded by sup⁡∣g′∣ ∣f(τ)∣\sup\abs{g'}\,\abs{f(\tau)}sup∣g′∣∣f(τ)∣, an integrable function that does not depend on ttt. The integral defining (f∗g)(t)(f\conv g)(t)(f∗g)(t) converges absolutely by Proposition 25.2. Rule I2 of Lecture 22 shows that f∗gf\conv gf∗g is continuously differentiable with the derivative ∫f(τ)g′(t−τ) ⁣dτ=(f∗g′)(t)\int f(\tau)g'(t-\tau)\dd\tau=(f\conv g')(t)∫f(τ)g′(t−τ)dτ=(f∗g′)(t). ■

Every derivative of the Gaussian ησ\eta_\sigmaησ​ of Example 25.5 is a polynomial times ησ\eta_\sigmaησ​, hence bounded and integrable. Repeated use of the proposition shows that the smoothed signal f∗ησf\conv\eta_\sigmaf∗ησ​ is infinitely differentiable for every integrable fff.

25.4 Parseval and Plancherel

We now compare the size of a signal, measured by an integral of the squared modulus, with the size of its spectrum.

Definition 25.8 (Square-integrable functions and their inner product). A function fff that is piecewise continuous on every bounded interval is square-integrable on R\RR if ∫R∣f∣2 ⁣dt<∞\int_{\R}\abs f^2\dd t<\infty∫R​∣f∣2dt<∞. For square-integrable fff and ggg the inner product and the norm are ⟨f,g⟩=∫Rf(t)‾ g(t) ⁣dt,∥f∥=(∫R∣f(t)∣2 ⁣dt)1/2.\inner fg=\int_{\R}\conj{f(t)}\,g(t)\dd t,\qquad \norm f=\Bigl(\int_{\R}\abs{f(t)}^2\dd t\Bigr)^{1/2} .⟨f,g⟩=∫R​f(t)​g(t)dt,∥f∥=(∫R​∣f(t)∣2dt)1/2.

The inner product converges absolutely, because ∣f‾g∣≤(∣f∣2+∣g∣2)/2\abs{\conj fg}\le(\abs f^2+\abs g^2)/2​f​g​≤(∣f∣2+∣g∣2)/2. It is conjugate-linear in its first argument and linear in its second, as in LA 13. It differs from the linear pairing ⟨T,ψ⟩\distpair T\psi⟨T,ψ⟩ of Lecture 22, which has no conjugation. A piecewise continuous function that vanishes except at one point has norm zero. When we use the inner product and the norm, we therefore identify two functions that differ only at finitely many points in each bounded interval. A bounded integrable function is square-integrable, because ∣f∣2≤sup⁡∣f∣ ∣f∣\abs f^2\le\sup\abs f\,\abs f∣f∣2≤sup∣f∣∣f∣. For a voltage f(t)f(t)f(t) across a unit resistor, ∥f∥2\norm f^2∥f∥2 is the energy dissipated, and we call ∥f∥2\norm f^2∥f∥2 the energy of the signal.

We also use the reflected conjugate f~(t)=f(−t)‾,F ⁣[f~](ω)=f^(ω)‾.\tilde f(t)=\conj{f(-t)},\qquad \FT{\tilde f}(\omega)=\conj{\widehat f(\omega)} .f~​(t)=f(−t)​,F[f~​](ω)=f​(ω)​.(25.10) The formula for its transform follows from Lecture 24’s reflection and conjugation rules. With g=f(−⋅)g=f(-\cdot)g=f(−⋅) the reflection rule gives g^(ω)=f^(−ω)\widehat g(\omega)=\widehat f(-\omega)g​(ω)=f​(−ω), and since f~=g‾\tilde f=\conj gf~​=g​, the conjugation rule gives F ⁣[f~](ω)=g^(−ω)‾=f^(ω)‾\FT{\tilde f}(\omega)=\conj{\widehat g(-\omega)}=\conj{\widehat f(\omega)}F[f~​](ω)=g​(−ω)​=f​(ω)​.

f~(t)=f(−t)‾,F ⁣[f~](ω)=f^(ω)‾.\tilde f(t)=\conj{f(-t)},\qquad \FT{\tilde f}(\omega)=\conj{\widehat f(\omega)} .f~​(t)=f(−t)​,F[f~​](ω)=f​(ω)​.(25.10)

Theorem 25.9 (Plancherel’s identity). Let fff be bounded and integrable on R\RR. Then ∣f^∣2\abs{\widehat f}^2​f​​2 is integrable on R\RR, and ∫R∣f^(ω)∣2 ⁣dω=∫R∣f(t)∣2 ⁣dt.\int_{\R}\abs{\widehat f(\omega)}^2\dd\omega=\int_{\R}\abs{f(t)}^2\dd t .∫R​​f​(ω)​2dω=∫R​∣f(t)∣2dt.(25.11)

Put E=∫∣f∣2 ⁣dtE=\int\abs f^2\dd tE=∫∣f∣2dt, and for ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 Aε=∫R∣f^(ω)∣2e−εω2/2 ⁣dω.A_\varepsilon=\int_{\R}\abs{\widehat f(\omega)}^2\ee^{-\varepsilon\omega^2/2}\dd\omega .Aε​=∫R​​f​(ω)​2e−εω2/2dω. The energy of a signal equals the energy of its spectrum. So ∣f^(ω)∣2\abs{\widehat f(\omega)}^2​f​(ω)​2 is the energy per unit angular frequency, the energy spectral density of fff. This is the reading of Lecture 23.

Proposition 25.10 (Parseval’s identity). Let fff and ggg be bounded and integrable on R\RR. Then ⟨f,g⟩=⟨f^,g^⟩,that is,∫Rf(t)‾ g(t) ⁣dt=∫Rf^(ω)‾ g^(ω) ⁣dω.\inner fg=\inner{\widehat f}{\widehat g},\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad \int_{\R}\conj{f(t)}\,g(t)\dd t=\int_{\R}\conj{\widehat f(\omega)}\,\widehat g(\omega)\dd\omega .⟨f,g⟩=⟨f​,g​⟩,that is,∫R​f(t)​g(t)dt=∫R​f​(ω)​g​(ω)dω.(25.12)

Proof. For complex numbers z1z_1z1​ and z2z_2z2​, expanding the squared moduli gives the polarization identity z1‾z2=14(∣z1+z2∣2−∣z1−z2∣2+i∣z1−iz2∣2−i∣z1+iz2∣2).\conj{z_1}z_2=\frac14\Bigl(\abs{z_1+z_2}^2-\abs{z_1-z_2}^2+\iu\abs{z_1-\iu z_2}^2-\iu\abs{z_1+\iu z_2}^2\Bigr) .z1​​z2​=41​(∣z1​+z2​∣2−∣z1​−z2​∣2+i∣z1​−iz2​∣2−i∣z1​+iz2​∣2). The four functions f+gf+gf+g, f−gf-gf−g, f−igf-\iu gf−ig and f+igf+\iu gf+ig are bounded and integrable, and their transforms are f^+g^\widehat f+\widehat gf​+g​, …, by linearity. Theorem 25.9 applies to each of them. Applying the identity with z1=f(t)z_1=f(t)z1​=f(t), z2=g(t)z_2=g(t)z2​=g(t) and with z1=f^(ω)z_1=\widehat f(\omega)z1​=f​(ω), z2=g^(ω)z_2=\widehat g(\omega)z2​=g​(ω), and integrating, gives (25.12). ■

Example 25.11 (The energy of a pulse). We apply Plancherel’s identity to a pulse. The pulse Πa\Pi_aΠa​ of Lecture 23, with a>0a>0a>0, is bounded and integrable, its energy is 2a2a2a, and ∣Πa^(ω)∣2=(2/π)sin⁡2(aω)/ω2\abs{\widehat{\Pi_a}(\omega)}^2=(2/\pi)\sin^2(a\omega)/\omega^2​Πa​​(ω)​2=(2/π)sin2(aω)/ω2 for ω≠0\omega\ne0ω=0. The identity gives ∫Rsin⁡2(aω)ω2 ⁣dω=πa.\int_{\R}\frac{\sin^2(a\omega)}{\omega^2}\dd\omega=\pi a .∫R​ω2sin2(aω)​dω=πa.(25.13) The pulse spectrum sin⁡(aω)/ω\sin(a\omega)/\omegasin(aω)/ω is not integrable, but its square is. ◃

∫Rsin⁡2(aω)ω2 ⁣dω=πa.\int_{\R}\frac{\sin^2(a\omega)}{\omega^2}\dd\omega=\pi a .∫R​ω2sin2(aω)​dω=πa.(25.13)

Plancherel’s identity extends to functions that are square-integrable but not integrable, with the Lebesgue integral of the sibling course.

Theorem 25.12 (Plancherel for square-integrable functions · cited). Let fff be square-integrable on R\RR, and for R>0R>0R>0 put f^R(ω)=12π∫−RRe−iωtf(t) ⁣dt.\widehat f_R(\omega)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-R}^R\ee^{-\iu\omega t}f(t)\dd t .f​R​(ω)=2π​1​∫−RR​e−iωtf(t)dt. There is a function f^\widehat ff​ in the Lebesgue space L2(R)L^2(\R)L2(R) of Real and Complex Analysis, the transform of fff, such that ∫∣f^R−f^∣2 ⁣dω→0\int\abs{\widehat f_R-\widehat f}^2\dd\omega\to0∫​f​R​−f​​2dω→0 as R→∞R\to\inftyR→∞, and ∫∣f^∣2 ⁣dω=∫∣f∣2 ⁣dt\int\abs{\widehat f}^2\dd\omega=\int\abs f^2\dd t∫​f​​2dω=∫∣f∣2dt. Parseval’s identity (25.12) holds for two such functions. If fff is also integrable, f^\widehat ff​ may be taken to be the transform of Lecture 23.

The sibling course proves this in AN 7’s theorem “Plancherel”: the transform extends to a unitary map of L2(R)L^2(\R)L2(R) that agrees almost everywhere with the integral transform on functions that are both integrable and square-integrable. Here a property holds almost everywhere if it fails only on a set of measure zero (a null set, AN 3), and L2(R)L^2(\R)L2(R) consists of the functions with ∫∣f∣2<∞\int\abs f^2<\infty∫∣f∣2<∞ in the sense of AN’s Lebesgue integral, a wider class than that of Definition 25.8; two functions are the same element of L2(R)L^2(\R)L2(R) when they agree almost everywhere (AN 5). The truncations fΠRf\Pi_RfΠR​ have the transforms f^R\widehat f_Rf​R​ and tend to fff in the mean, ∫∣f−fΠR∣2 ⁣dt→0\int\abs{f-f\Pi_R}^2\dd t\to0∫∣f−fΠR​∣2dt→0; unitarity carries this convergence to the transforms. Convergence in the mean is an integral statement and does not see values at finitely many points.

25.5 Correlation

A convolution describes what a device does to a signal. A correlation measures how similar two signals are when one of them is shifted in time.

Definition 25.13 (Cross-correlation and autocorrelation). Let fff and ggg be bounded and integrable on R\RR. Their cross-correlation is the function of the lag u∈Ru\in\Ru∈R given by Cfg(u)=∫Rf(t)‾ g(t+u) ⁣dt.C_{fg}(u)=\int_{\R}\conj{f(t)}\,g(t+u)\dd t .Cfg​(u)=∫R​f(t)​g(t+u)dt.(25.14) The autocorrelation of fff is CffC_{ff}Cff​.

The conjugation is on the first function, as in the inner product: Cfg(u)=⟨f,g(⋅+u)⟩C_{fg}(u)=\inner{f}{g(\cdot+u)}Cfg​(u)=⟨f,g(⋅+u)⟩. The lag uuu shifts the second function to earlier times. With the reflected conjugate (25.10), the substitution t=−τt=-\taut=−τ gives Cfg(u)=∫Rf~(τ) g(u−τ) ⁣dτ=(f~∗g)(u).C_{fg}(u)=\int_{\R}\tilde f(\tau)\,g(u-\tau)\dd\tau=(\tilde f\conv g)(u) .Cfg​(u)=∫R​f~​(τ)g(u−τ)dτ=(f~​∗g)(u).(25.15) So CfgC_{fg}Cfg​ is continuous, bounded and integrable by Proposition 25.2. The comparison of two signals rests on the following inequality.

Cfg(u)=∫Rf~(τ) g(u−τ) ⁣dτ=(f~∗g)(u).C_{fg}(u)=\int_{\R}\tilde f(\tau)\,g(u-\tau)\dd\tau=(\tilde f\conv g)(u) .Cfg​(u)=∫R​f~​(τ)g(u−τ)dτ=(f~​∗g)(u).(25.15)

Lemma 25.14 (Cauchy–Schwarz inequality). For square-integrable fff and ggg, ∣⟨f,g⟩∣≤∥f∥ ∥g∥\abs{\inner fg}\le\norm f\,\norm g∣⟨f,g⟩∣≤∥f∥∥g∥.

Proof. Let α>0\alpha>0α>0. The inequality 2xy≤αx2+y2/α2xy\le\alpha x^2+y^2/\alpha2xy≤αx2+y2/α for real xxx and yyy, and then Lecture 17’s inequality ∣∫⋯ ∣≤∫∣⋯ ∣\abs{\int\cdots}\le\int\abs{\cdots}​∫⋯​≤∫∣⋯∣, give ∣f‾g∣≤12(α∣f∣2+∣g∣2α),∣⟨f,g⟩∣≤12(α∥f∥2+∥g∥2α).\abs{\conj fg}\le\frac12\Bigl(\alpha\abs f^2+\frac{\abs g^2}\alpha\Bigr),\qquad \abs{\inner fg}\le\frac12\Bigl(\alpha\norm f^2+\frac{\norm g^2}\alpha\Bigr).​f​g​≤21​(α∣f∣2+α∣g∣2​),∣⟨f,g⟩∣≤21​(α∥f∥2+α∥g∥2​). If ∥f∥>0\norm f>0∥f∥>0 and ∥g∥>0\norm g>0∥g∥>0, the choice α=∥g∥/∥f∥\alpha=\norm g/\norm fα=∥g∥/∥f∥ gives the claim. If ∥f∥=0\norm f=0∥f∥=0, letting α→∞\alpha\to\inftyα→∞ gives ⟨f,g⟩=0\inner fg=0⟨f,g⟩=0; if ∥g∥=0\norm g=0∥g∥=0, let α→0+\alpha\to0^+α→0+. ■

This is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality of LA 13 (Example “Cauchy–Schwarz for integrals”) for our class of functions.

Proposition 25.15 (Properties of correlations). Let fff and ggg be bounded and integrable on R\RR, and let u∈Ru\in\Ru∈R. Then Cgf(u)=Cfg(−u)‾,Cff(0)=∥f∥2,∣Cff(u)∣≤Cff(0).C_{gf}(u)=\conj{C_{fg}(-u)},\qquad C_{ff}(0)=\norm f^2,\qquad \abs{C_{ff}(u)}\le C_{ff}(0) .Cgf​(u)=Cfg​(−u)​,Cff​(0)=∥f∥2,∣Cff​(u)∣≤Cff​(0). If g(t)=f(t−t0)g(t)=f(t-t_0)g(t)=f(t−t0​) for a delay t0∈Rt_0\in\Rt0​∈R, then Cfg(u)=Cff(u−t0)C_{fg}(u)=C_{ff}(u-t_0)Cfg​(u)=Cff​(u−t0​), and ∣Cfg∣\abs{C_{fg}}∣Cfg​∣ attains its largest value ∥f∥2\norm f^2∥f∥2 at u=t0u=t_0u=t0​.

Proof. The substitution t=v−ut=v-ut=v−u gives Cgf(u)=∫g(v−u)‾f(v) ⁣dvC_{gf}(u)=\int\conj{g(v-u)}f(v)\dd vCgf​(u)=∫g(v−u)​f(v)dv, the conjugate of ∫f(v)‾g(v−u) ⁣dv=Cfg(−u)\int\conj{f(v)}g(v-u)\dd v=C_{fg}(-u)∫f(v)​g(v−u)dv=Cfg​(−u). The second formula is the definition at u=0u=0u=0. For the inequality, the shifted function f(⋅+u)f(\cdot+u)f(⋅+u) has the same norm as fff (substitution), so Lemma 25.14 gives ∣Cff(u)∣≤∥f∥ ∥f(⋅+u)∥=∥f∥2\abs{C_{ff}(u)}\le\norm f\,\norm{f(\cdot+u)}=\norm f^2∣Cff​(u)∣≤∥f∥∥f(⋅+u)∥=∥f∥2. For the delayed signal, Cfg(u)=∫f(t)‾f(t+u−t0) ⁣dt=Cff(u−t0)C_{fg}(u)=\int\conj{f(t)}f(t+u-t_0)\dd t=C_{ff}(u-t_0)Cfg​(u)=∫f(t)​f(t+u−t0​)dt=Cff​(u−t0​), and the inequality just proved gives the last claim. ■

The last statement is the principle of echo ranging: a pulse fff is sent, its echo ggg returns after the delay t0t_0t0​, and the cross-correlation of the two records peaks at the lag u=t0u=t_0u=t0​, which measures the time of flight.

Theorem 25.16 (Correlation theorem). Let fff and ggg be bounded and integrable on R\RR. Then F ⁣[Cfg](ω)=2π f^(ω)‾ g^(ω),F ⁣[Cff](ω)=2π ∣f^(ω)∣2,\FT{C_{fg}}(\omega)=\sqrt{2\pi}\,\conj{\widehat f(\omega)}\,\widehat g(\omega),\qquad \FT{C_{ff}}(\omega)=\sqrt{2\pi}\,\abs{\widehat f(\omega)}^2 ,F[Cfg​](ω)=2π​f​(ω)​g​(ω),F[Cff​](ω)=2π​​f​(ω)​2,(25.16) and for every u∈Ru\in\Ru∈R Cff(u)=∫Reiωu ∣f^(ω)∣2 ⁣dω.C_{ff}(u)=\int_{\R}\ee^{\iu\omega u}\,\abs{\widehat f(\omega)}^2\dd\omega .Cff​(u)=∫R​eiωu​f​(ω)​2dω.(25.17)

The autocorrelation CffC_{ff}Cff​ is continuous and integrable, and its transform 2π∣f^∣2\sqrt{2\pi}\abs{\widehat f}^22π​​f​​2 is integrable by Theorem 25.9. So Lecture 23’s inversion theorem applies and gives Cff(u)=(2π)−1/2∫eiωu2π∣f^(ω)∣2 ⁣dωC_{ff}(u)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int\ee^{\iu\omega u}\sqrt{2\pi}\abs{\widehat f(\omega)}^2\dd\omegaCff​(u)=(2π)−1/2∫eiωu2π​​f​(ω)​2dω, which is (25.17). ■

Formula (25.17) is the deterministic form of the Wiener–Khinchin relation: the autocorrelation and 2π\sqrt{2\pi}2π​ times the energy spectral density are a transform pair. At u=0u=0u=0 it is Plancherel’s identity. The autocorrelation does not see the phase of the spectrum: fff and its delayed copy f(⋅−t0)f(\cdot-t_0)f(⋅−t0​) have the same autocorrelation. A stationary random signal need not have finite energy; its correlation is defined through an expectation instead (Part IV).

Example 25.17 (The correlation of a damped oscillation). 25.6 Convolution integral equations

The second worked example of the lecture is an equation for an unknown function that appears under a convolution integral. Summary

The transform turns a convolution into a product. So a linear device with the impulse response hhh multiplies the spectrum of its input by 2π h^\sqrt{2\pi}\,\widehat h2π​h, an energy or a correlation can be computed from the spectrum, and a convolution equation whose multiplier has no real zero is solved by division.

  • Convolution: (f∗g)(t)=∫f(τ)g(t−τ) ⁣dτ(f\conv g)(t)=\int f(\tau)g(t-\tau)\dd\tau(f∗g)(t)=∫f(τ)g(t−τ)dτ; for fff integrable and ggg bounded and integrable, F ⁣[f∗g]=2πf^g^\FT{f\conv g}=\sqrt{2\pi}\widehat f\widehat gF[f∗g]=2π​f​g​; for causal signals the integral runs over [0,t][0,t][0,t].

  • Uniqueness: if integrable fff and ggg have equal transforms, then f=gf=gf=g at every point of continuity of f−gf-gf−g.

  • Energy: for bounded integrable fff and ggg, ∫∣f^∣2 ⁣dω=∫∣f∣2 ⁣dt\int\abs{\widehat f}^2\dd\omega=\int\abs f^2\dd t∫​f​​2dω=∫∣f∣2dt and ⟨f,g⟩=⟨f^,g^⟩\inner fg=\inner{\widehat f}{\widehat g}⟨f,g⟩=⟨f​,g​⟩.

  • Correlation: Cfg(u)=∫f(t)‾g(t+u) ⁣dtC_{fg}(u)=\int\conj{f(t)}g(t+u)\dd tCfg​(u)=∫f(t)​g(t+u)dt, F ⁣[Cfg]=2πf^‾g^\FT{C_{fg}}=\sqrt{2\pi}\conj{\widehat f}\widehat gF[Cfg​]=2π​f​​g​, Cff(u)=∫eiωu∣f^∣2 ⁣dωC_{ff}(u)=\int\ee^{\iu\omega u}\abs{\widehat f}^2\dd\omegaCff​(u)=∫eiωu​f​​2dω, ∣Cff(u)∣≤Cff(0)=∥f∥2\abs{C_{ff}(u)}\le C_{ff}(0)=\norm f^2∣Cff​(u)∣≤Cff​(0)=∥f∥2.

  • Integral equations: y=f+λ y∗Ky=f+\lambda\,y\conv Ky=f+λy∗K has at most one bounded integrable solution if 1−λ2πK^(ω)≠01-\lambda\sqrt{2\pi}\widehat K(\omega)\ne01−λ2π​K(ω)=0 for every real ω\omegaω; with a resolvent kernel the solution is f+f∗Rλf+f\conv R_\lambdaf+f∗Rλ​.

Lecture 26 turns to one-sided transforms of causal signals with a complex variable, in which a convolution again becomes a product.
